claims.claim: Correlation describes the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables; it takes values on a scale from -1 to +1, where the ends mark perfect patterns in opposite and same directions and zero marks no straight-line pattern.

A positive correlation means the variables move in the same direction, high values of one occurring with high values of the other; a negative correlation means they move in opposite directions, high values of one occurring with low values of the other.
The strength of a correlation is how closely the points cluster around the trend: tightly clustered points indicate a strong relationship, widely scattered points a weak one.

A scatterplot plots one point per observation, positioned by its two variable values on two axes, and is the standard way to reveal whether and how two variables are related; relationships appear as non-random structure in the plot.
No statistical procedure, including the scatterplot and correlation measures, can prove cause and effect; establishing causation requires reasoning beyond statistics.
Ice cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer; the correlation does not mean ice cream causes drowning, because warm weather is a third variable that drives both.
A third variable (also called a lurking or confounding variable) can affect both observed variables and create a correlation that neither one causes.
Reverse causation is the situation in which the apparent direction of a relationship is backward, so that the second variable actually influences the first.
A correlation can also be coincidental: two unrelated series moving together by chance.
Correlation measures straight-line patterns, so a strong nonlinear relationship can produce a weak correlation; the chart should be inspected rather than relying on the number alone.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strong a correlation must be before it is called "strong" has no universal cutoff; authoritative sources describe strength relative to how tightly points cluster, while some introductory materials offer informal rule-of-thumb ranges.
positions: OpenIntro IMS and the OnlineStatBook describe strength qualitatively in terms of clustering around the trend without fixed thresholds
Some introductory materials suggest informal benchmarks (e.g., rough numeric bands) for strong/moderate/weak
NIST e-Handbook presents scatter-plot patterns (strong positive, strong negative, no relationship) without numeric cutoffs
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes strength qualitatively (tight versus loose clustering) and explicitly avoids numeric cutoffs, which keeps it accurate at the literacy level.

sourceRecords.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — 1.3.3.26. Scatter Plot
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21 (Section 1.3.3.26). Supports: a scatter plot reveals relationships or association between two variables, which manifest as any non-random structure in the plot; scatter plots are the cornerstone EDA tool for uncovering relationships; no statistical procedure, scatter plot included, proves cause-and-effect, and such proof is beyond the realm of statistics. Facts synthesized; no page wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: OpenIntro — Introduction to Modern Statistics (2e), Section 7.1: Fitting a line, residuals, and correlation
sourceRecords.notes: Read live web edition 2026-08-21 (Chapter 7, Section 7.1.4). Supports: correlation takes values between -1 and 1 and describes the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables; strong positive relationships are near +1, strong negative near -1, no apparent linear relationship near zero; correlation is unitless; nonlinear trends can produce correlations that do not reflect the strength of the relationship; correlation does not specify which variable is explanatory and which is outcome. No source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Online Statistics Education: An Interactive Multimedia Course of Study — Describing Bivariate Data: Introduction
sourceRecords.provider: Rice University (Rudy Guerra and David M. Lane)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-21 (Chapter 4). Supports: bivariate data pairs two quantitative variables per individual; when Y increases as X increases the association is positive, when Y decreases as X increases it is negative; points clustering along a line indicate a linear relationship; strength is visible in how closely points cluster; pairing is lost when variables are summarized separately. No explicit license statement found on the page; used as reference only, prose fully original.

sourceRecords.title: Correlation does not imply causation
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Tier D reference used for the classic ice-cream-sales/drowning-rates illustration (summer heat as the common cause) and the named alternative explanations: third factor (common-cause variable, lurking/confounding variable), reverse causation, and coincidence. Causal-inference claims in the lesson are additionally anchored to the NIST e-Handbook statement that no statistical procedure proves cause and effect.
